candidates.attacker_control: The `redirectedFrom` request parameter (query string or POST body) is fully attacker-controlled. A value such as `redirectedFrom=https://attacker.example/login` (or any absolute http(s) URL) is accepted; the value is also stored in the view model on the GET path.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that the GET handler validates the parameter (`equals("appointmentBlockCalendar.list")`), showing validation was intended; checked all other `redirect:` usages in the module (static/internal views); checked that `required=false` only means the parameter may be absent (absent value yields the harmless literal "redirect:null"); checked that Spring's default `redirectContextRelative=true` only prefixes context paths to URLs starting with '/', so absolute external URLs are honored (version-dependent behaviour not runtime-verified). Also considered impact limits: no privilege escalation or data access by itself.
candidates.impact: Open redirect / phishing: an attacker can use the trusted OpenMRS host to bounce authenticated users to an attacker-controlled page (e.g. a fake login form) after they submit the appointment-block form. No direct data or integrity impact was identified; secondary impact depends on how the parameter is rendered in the (not included) JSP.
candidates.prerequisites: A request must reach the module's Spring MVC dispatcher for POST /openmrs/module/appointmentscheduling/appointmentBlockForm.form; in default OpenMRS deployments module pages normally sit behind authentication, so exploitation is typically post-authentication and requires inducing the victim's browser to issue the POST (e.g. an auto-submitting cross-site form). No application privilege beyond an authenticated session appears to be required, since the redirect statement is outside the controller's `Context.isAuthenticated()` branch and no service call is needed to reach it.
candidates.root_cause: In the POST handler `onSubmit`, the request parameter `redirectedFrom` is bound with `@RequestParam(required = false)` and used directly to build the view name: `return "redirect:" + redirectedFrom;` (line 313). There is no whitelist/format validation and the concatenation happens outside the `if (Context.isAuthenticated())` block, so the value fully controls the redirect target. The GET handler in the same controller (lines 79-95) shows the intended behaviour: it only treats the parameter as meaningful when `redirectedFrom.equals("appointmentBlockCalendar.list")`, i.e. the value is expected to be one of a few fixed internal page names; all other redirects in the module are static strings (e.g. AppointmentBlockListController line 160/165, AppointmentBlockCalendarController lines 163/167/171).
candidates.title: Unvalidated `redirectedFrom` parameter allows open redirect in AppointmentBlockFormController
candidates.trace: HTTP POST with `redirectedFrom=<absolute URL>` -> AppointmentBlockFormController.onSubmit binds the parameter (line 157) -> `return "redirect:" + redirectedFrom;` (line 313) -> Spring `UrlBasedViewResolver` detects the `redirect:` prefix and creates a `RedirectView`; because Spring only prepends the context path to URLs beginning with '/', an absolute URL is passed through unchanged -> `HttpServletResponse.sendRedirect` emits a `Location: https://attacker.example/...` header -> the victim's browser is redirected off-site.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed. Spring/OpenMRS URL resolution and whether module pages are reachable without authentication were not executed or inspected (OpenMRS core is an external dependency not present in the snapshot). The GET path also writes the raw parameter into the model; whether the corresponding (excluded) JSP escapes it when rendering a hidden field — a possible reflected XSS — could not be verified because JSPs are not part of this snapshot.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-601: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect')

coverage_summary: Scope per get_source_scope: 191 readable files, no over-size or sensitive-path exclusions; binary-like files are skipped by the tools. Reviewed all Java sources under api/ and omod/ (service interface and impl, REST resources/controllers/search handler, Hibernate DAOs and HQL/raw-SQL query construction, validators/editors, DWR service, reporting data/query evaluators), moduleApplicationContext.xml, webModuleApplicationContext.xml, config.xml (privileges, DWR allow-list, mappings), all *.hbm.xml mappings, messages.properties, and Liquibase changesets (searched for privilege/role and column changes). Spot-checked bundled JS/CSS libraries. No JSP/view files and no test sources are present in the snapshot, and OpenMRS core (the source of most @Authorized semantics and web filters) is an external dependency not included.
limitations: No JSP/pages or test sources in the snapshot, so output-side rendering (XSS) and intended privilege tests could not be inspected.

OpenMRS core sources (Context/@Authorized interception, AuthenticationFilter behavior, PatientService/VisitService/ProviderService annotations) are not available; their authorization behavior is reasoned about, not verified.
No runtime, build, or dependency access: Spring version behavior for `redirect:`/RedirectView and the exact servlet/filter chain could not be confirmed by execution.
Line numbers refer to the snapshot as read; generated/assembled files (@MODULE_PACKAGE@ placeholders) are resolved at build time.
The single-candidate cap means other plausible authorization weaknesses are reported only as rejected/unconfirmed leads.

rejected_leads.lead: Confidential appointments not filtered in the REST/web read paths: AppointmentType.confidential / AppointmentSchedulingConstants.PRIVILEGE_VIEW_CONFIDENTIAL_APPOINTMENT_DETAILS ('Task: appointmentschedulingui.viewConfidential') is enforced only in PatientToAppointmentDataEvaluator and PersonToAppointmentDataEvaluator (reporting), while AppointmentResource1_9.doSearch/doGetAll and AppointmentListController return confidential appointments to any user with 'View Appointments'.
rejected_leads.reason: Potentially high impact (patient/appointment details) but the intended enforcement boundary is ambiguous: the legacy list path never filters either, the privilege name is namespaced to the separate appointmentschedulingui module (which may filter client/server-side), and no in-repo comment states that this REST API must filter. Flagged as a lead needing deployment-context confirmation, not submitted as the candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Missing privilege on ProviderSchedule REST lookup: AppointmentService.getProviderScheduleByUuid is annotated only @Authorized() (any authenticated user) although sibling methods require 'View Provider Scedules'/'View Provider Schedules' and config.xml defines the view privilege; it is exposed via GET /rest/v1/appointmentscheduling/providerschedule/{uuid}.
rejected_leads.reason: Real-looking authorization oversight but low impact (provider schedule metadata); additionally the module's own PRIV_VIEW/MANAGE_PROVIDER_SCHEDULES constants are misspelled ('Scedules') versus config.xml, so the intended privilege checks in siblings are themselves broken, making the 'intended' control unclear.

rejected_leads.lead: Overbooking without the 'Squeezing Appointments' privilege: AppointmentAllowingOverbookResource1_9 -> AppointmentResource1_9.save(appointment, true) -> bookAppointment(..., true) skips the capacity check and requires only 'Schedule Appointments'; PRIV_SQUEEZE_APPOINTMENTS is checked only in the web UI (AppointmentFormController line 135).
rejected_leads.reason: Privilege description ('override the constraints and schedule appointments into full slots') matches the bypassed check, but the UI-only check may be deliberate (privilege used as a UI affordance), so the intent violation is not established with sufficient confidence.

rejected_leads.lead: Unauthorized creation of AppointmentBlock/TimeSlot rows: AppointmentRequisitionController (POST /rest/v1/appointmentscheduling/createappointment) calls getTimeslotForAppointment and createTimeSlotUsingProviderSchedule (both only @Authorized()) before bookAppointment enforces 'Schedule Appointments'; createTimeSlotUsingProviderSchedule writes blocks/slots directly through the DAOs.
rejected_leads.reason: State-changing side effect occurs before the scheduling privilege check, but reachability requires several core-level view privileges and knowledge of provider/location/patient UUIDs; impact and exploitability are speculative without the OpenMRS core authorization annotations.

rejected_leads.lead: Appointment status changes require only 'Schedule Appointments' (changeAppointmentStatus, AppointmentResource1_9 update path) while the module defines a separate 'Update Appointment Status' privilege used only for rendering dashboard buttons.
rejected_leads.reason: Overlapping privilege semantics likely intentional (scheduling staff are expected to update statuses); insufficient evidence of an unintended privilege boundary.

rejected_leads.lead: Possible reflected XSS: the GET handler stores the raw `redirectedFrom` value in the model (AppointmentBlockFormController line 94), and the hidden form field could render it unescaped.
rejected_leads.reason: Cannot be verified: JSP/page files are not included in this snapshot, so the output context and escaping are unknown.

summary: Reviewed the OpenMRS Appointment Scheduling module snapshot (191 readable files: api + omod Java sources, Spring/module XML, Hibernate mappings, Liquibase, JS resources). No SQL/HQL injection or deserialization sinks were found (all DAO queries are parameterized); privilege enforcement is mostly at the service interface via @Authorized. The single strongest, most concrete candidate is an open redirect in AppointmentBlockFormController: the POST handler concatenates the raw, unvalidated request parameter `redirectedFrom` into a Spring `redirect:` view name, while the GET handler of the same controller validates that parameter against exactly one expected value. Other plausible but weaker/unconfirmed leads (missing view privilege on ProviderSchedule lookup, overbooking without the "Squeezing Appointments" privilege, missing confidential-appointment filtering in REST/list paths, unauthorized block/time-slot creation via the createappointment requisition endpoint) are recorded as rejected leads rather than additional candidates.
